paragraphs.text: A gene is a DNA sequence associated with a functional product or characteristic. Alternative versions are alleles. In a diploid autosomal model, an individual inherits one allele from each parent and therefore has two alleles at the locus being studied.

The genotype is the allele combination, such as BB, Bb or bb. The phenotype is the observed or measured characteristic, such as dark or pale pigment. A phenotype can also be an enzyme activity or another physiological property, not only a visible feature.

Suppose a stated model says B gives dark pigment and is completely dominant to b. BB and Bb individuals have the dark phenotype, while bb individuals have the pale phenotype. The same phenotype can therefore correspond to more than one genotype.

Homozygous means the two alleles are the same, as in BB or bb. Heterozygous means they differ, as in Bb. A dominant allele is expressed in the heterozygote under the stated complete-dominance model. Dominant does not mean most common, healthiest or strongest.

Use the inheritance model supplied. Many traits involve multiple genes, environmental influences or allele relationships other than complete dominance. Do not assume that human eye colour can be accurately predicted by a single B/b model.

Define letters before solving a problem. Use the same letter for alleles of one gene and a different letter for a different gene. A capital and lowercase letter are convenient for a complete-dominance model; other models use different notation.

A useful first question is whether the phenotype determines a unique genotype. A recessive phenotype in a simple fully expressed model identifies bb. A dominant phenotype alone leaves BB or Bb possible. Keeping that uncertainty visible prevents an incorrect cross from the start.

Mendel studied traits in pea plants and used controlled crosses between lines with contrasting forms. In a simple example, let R represent round seeds and r wrinkled seeds, with complete dominance of R. A true-breeding RR line crossed with rr produces Rr offspring in the F1 generation.
Every F1 individual can have the round phenotype while still carrying the r allele. The recessive allele has not disappeared or blended into a weaker version. It remains part of the genotype.
An Rr individual forms gametes containing R or r. The alleles segregate as homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis. In the simple model, each allele has a one-half chance of entering a gamete.

When two Rr individuals produce the F2 generation, gametes can combine as RR, Rr, rR or rr. Rr and rR name the same heterozygous genotype. The expected genotype ratio is 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr. With complete dominance, the expected phenotype ratio is 3 round : 1 wrinkled.
The wrinkled phenotype reappears because an offspring can receive r from both parents. No new r mutation is required to explain that result.

A 3:1 expected ratio is not a promise that every group of four offspring contains exactly three round and one wrinkled. Each offspring is another event. Chance variation is especially noticeable in small samples.

Mendel's repeated patterns supported a particulate model of inheritance: inherited units remain distinguishable rather than permanently blending. Later chromosome and DNA evidence connected those units with cellular mechanisms.

When interpreting a cross, identify the parental genotypes, gamete possibilities and allele combinations before applying the phenotype rule. A remembered ratio should be the result of that reasoning, not a substitute for it.

A Punnett square organizes combinations of gametes. For Aa × aa, the first parent produces A or a gametes; the second produces only a. Place those gametes on the edges and combine one from each parent in each cell.

The resulting possibilities are Aa and aa in equal proportions. With complete dominance, half are expected to have the dominant phenotype and half the recessive phenotype. The square shows why the 1:1 ratio applies; a 3:1 ratio would be the wrong shortcut for this cross.

For Aa × Aa, the four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa. Grouping the two heterozygous combinations gives probabilities of 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa and 1/4 aa. The dominant phenotype has probability 3/4 under complete dominance.

Genotype probability and phenotype probability therefore can differ. “Heterozygous” refers to two of the four combinations, while “dominant phenotype” includes three. Mark the requested group before choosing your numerator.
When converting to an expected number, multiply by the total. If 80 offspring each have a 1/4 chance of aa, the expected number is 80 × 0.25 = 20. The result is an expectation, not a promise.

In the simple model, one offspring's genotype does not force the next offspring to be different. If two Aa parents have several dominant-phenotype offspring, the modeled probability for the next offspring is still 1/4 recessive.

For specified independent events, multiply probabilities. Two recessive offspring in a row from Aa × Aa have probability 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Do not confuse this ordered event with “at least one recessive among two,” which asks for a different set of outcomes.
State assumptions such as complete dominance and ordinary segregation. They determine which genotype combinations count toward a phenotype.

An individual with a dominant phenotype may be AA or Aa. Crossing it with aa creates a useful test because the recessive tester can contribute only a. The phenotype of the offspring then provides evidence about the unknown parent's contribution.

If the unknown parent is AA, every offspring is expected to be Aa and show the dominant phenotype. If the unknown parent is Aa, the expected offspring are half Aa and half aa. A recessive offspring therefore demonstrates that the unknown parent contributed a, under the stated simple model.
One aa offspring from B_ × bb means the dominant-phenotype parent must carry the recessive allele, assuming the model, parentage and observations are correct. It is heterozygous.

By contrast, several dominant offspring do not logically prove the parent is homozygous. An Aa parent can, by chance, produce a run of A-bearing gametes. For four independent offspring in an Aa × aa cross, the probability that all show the dominant phenotype is (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.

More offspring with no recessive phenotype generally strengthen the homozygous interpretation, but finite samples still require cautious wording. Say what the evidence supports and what remains possible.

Additional parent or offspring information can resolve an unknown genotype. A dominant-phenotype individual with an aa parent must have received a from that parent, so it must be Aa. You do not need another test cross to establish that conclusion within the model.

Start with the most informative constraints. Write the alleles that must be present, preserve unknowns where necessary, and only then calculate the next cross. Guessing an unresolved genotype can make every later arithmetic step misleading.

For AaBb with independent assortment, choose one allele from the A/a pair and one from the B/b pair. The possible gametes are AB, Ab, aB and ab, each with probability 1/4. An Aabb parent has only Ab and ab as distinct possibilities.

Do not place Aa or Bb on a gamete edge. Those are two alleles of one locus, not one allele from each of two loci. A correctly sized square follows from the distinct gametes, not from a rule that every two-trait cross needs sixteen boxes.

For AaBb × AaBb, the A locus gives a 3/4 dominant-phenotype probability and 1/4 recessive probability. The B locus gives the same. If the loci assort independently, the probability of both dominant phenotypes is 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16.
The other phenotype combinations are 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16, producing the familiar 9:3:3:1 expectation. This ratio is specific to the stated heterozygote cross and allele relationships.
For a different cross, recompute. In AaBb × aaBb, probability of A_ is 1/2 and probability of B_ is 3/4, so both dominant phenotypes have probability 3/8. A memorized 9/16 would be wrong.

Genes close together on the same chromosome can be linked. Their gamete combinations may not occur equally, so the simple product calculation can fail. Later lessons will use offspring data to test this.

For now, state when independent assortment is assumed. Check that the probabilities of all mutually exclusive phenotype categories add to one. When calculating an expected count, multiply the appropriate probability by the total number of offspring.
Both the square and product method are tools for organizing the same biological possibilities. Choose the clearer method, but show enough steps that the allele contributions can be checked.
